Rust is a general-purpose language that balances performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. Its multi-paradigm design draws on functional ideas such as immutability and pattern matching [1].

Graydon Hoare started Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. It was first released publicly in 2010, with version 1.0 arriving in 2015 [2].

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java achieves this through runtime checks of array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. C, C++, and Fortran, by contrast, allow unchecked pointer arithmetic, which makes them memory-unsafe [3].

Rust's syntax resembles C++, yet it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2]. Rather than classes and inheritance, it relies on structs, enums, traits, and methods [1].

Adopters of Rust must weigh strong safety guarantees against a steeper learning curve.

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java achieves this through runtime checks of array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. C, C++, and Fortran, by contrast, allow unchecked pointer arithmetic, which makes them memory-unsafe [3].

Rust's syntax resembles C++, yet it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2]. Rather than classes and inheritance, it relies on structs, enums, traits, and methods [1].
